a false claim after concealing material facts and claim of the workman is not maintainable. 


11. I have given due consideration to the arguments advanced by AR for both the parties. 


Findings:- 

12. The first contention regarding the applicant is that whether applicant comes within the definition of 
workman as is defined in Section 2(s) of the Act. I may mention that applicant was appointed as sweeper as per his 
claim petition and affidavit submitted before the Tribunal. In plain words the applicant was performing his duties as 
labourer/unskilled worker. He was not in supervisory or administrative post requiring him to perform only 
administrative duties. While interpreting Section 2(s) Hon’ble Supreme Court in the case of Devinder Singh Vs. 
Municipal Council, Sanaur, AIR 2011 Supreme Court 2532, has observed as follows:- 


“The source of employment, the quantum of recruitment, the terms & conditions of employment contract of 
service, the quantum of wages/ pay and mode of payment are not at all relevant for deciding whether or not a 
person is a workman within the meaning of Section 2(s) of the Act. The definition of workman also does not 
make any distinction between full time and part time employee or a person appointed on contract basis. 
There is nothing in the plain language of Section 2(s) from which it can be inferred that only person 
employed on regular basis or a person employed for doing whole time job is a workman and the one 
employed on temporary, part time or contract basis on fixed wages or as a casual employee or for doing duty 
for fixed hours is not a workman.” 


13. Thus Hon’ble Supreme Court has clarified that the definition of workman also does not make any distinction 
between full time or part time employee or a person appointed on contract basis. There is nothing in plain language of 


1086 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : MARCHY 7, 2026/PHALGUNA 16, 1947 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 


Section 2(s) from which it can be infer that only person employed on regular basis or a person employed for doing 
whole time job is a workman and the one employed on temporary, part time or contract basis on fixed wages or as a 
casual employee or for doing duty for fixed hours is not a workman. In view of the ratio of law enunciated in the 
above ruling, in my considered opinion the applicant herein admittedly falls within the definition of ‘workman’ under 
Section 2(s) of the Act. 


14. The Hon’ble Supreme Court after analyzing the catena of cases has laid down in Balwant Raj Saluja Vs. Air 
India Limited in Civil Appeal No.10266 dated 25.08.2014, two well recognized tests to find out whether the labours 
are the contract employees of the principal employer are:- 


1) Whether the principal employer pays the salary instead of contractor and 
2) Whether the principal employer controls and supervise the work of the employees? 


15. The facts regarding the payment of salary by the management or contractor has not been stated in the claim 
petition of the workman. In fact, claim petition is totally silent regarding the payment of wages, salary, letter of 
appointment by respondent 10.1 or by contractor or anything likewise. Thus, this basic feature for holding the 
relationship of employer and employee i.e. between respondent 10.1 and workman totally lacking not in the pleading 
but also in the evidence submitted by the workman. However, MW1 Colonel K P Singh in his cross examination has 
stated that it is responsibility of the contractor to pay monthly wages to the conservancy staff provided by him. 
Respondent 10.1 has nothing to do with the minimum wages, DC rate to the conservancy staff. Contractor is 
responsible to give notice to the conservancy staff provided by him. Respondent 10.1 has no roll in terminating the 
services of the workman. Thus, it was the respondent no.2 who was required to ensure the payment of wages to the 
workers engaged by him from time to time. 


16. It is also added here that respondent 10.1 has also placed on record documents Ex.R-1 to Ex.R-4. Ex.R-2 is 
the contract agreement between respondent no.1 & 2. Thus, from the adduced evidence, it emerges that workman was 
paid salary by the contractor and he was being controlled and supervised by the contractor. Thus, there does not exist 
any relationship of employee and employer between the workman and respondent no.1. However, there exists relation 
of employee and employer between the workman and respondent no.2. 


17. It is also added here that as per definition of contractor as given in the Section 2(c) of the Contract Labour 
(Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970 (hereinafter called as Contract Act), respondent no.2 was supplying contract 
labour to the respondent no.1. Thus, respondent no.2 would fall under the definition of contractor. Section 2(c) of the 
Contract Act is reproduced as under: 


“Contractor”, in relation to an establishment, means a person who undertakes to produce a given result for the 
establishment, other than a mere supply of goods or articles of manufacture to such establishment, through contract 
labour or who supplies contract labour for any work of the establishment and includes a sub-contractor; 


18. The Hon’ble Apex Court in the case of Banglore Water Supply & Sewerage Board Vs. A. Rajappa 
1978(36) FLR 266 dealt at length with the ambit and scope of expression “industry” as defined in Section 2(j) of the 


Act, and has laid down triple test for determining whether a particular establishment is industry or not. The triple test 
is where (a) systematic activity (b) organized by cooperation between employer and employee (the direct and 
substantial element is commercial (c) for the production or distribution of goods and services to calculated to satisfy 
human wants and wishes prima facie is an “Industry” in that enterprise. The workman was doing work i.e. systematic 
activity for respondent no.1 at the asking of respondent no.2 and there was cooperation between the workman and 
respondent no.2, which involve substantial commercial element for rendering service to satisfy human wants. Thus, 
respondent no.2 would be termed as industry. 


19. Workman in his deposition has clearly stated that there was non-compliance of Section 259, 250 and 25H of 
the Act. He also stated that he was appointed on 09.09.2012 and he was paid minimum wages prescribed by Central 
Government and was working with respondent 10.1. He was not given any compensation before terminating his 
services on 27.10.2018. In his cross examination, he has further stated that his salary used to be credited in his bank 
account. But he has not placed on record any bank account, in which his salary was credited in order to enable this 
Court to see who was making payment to the workman. However, there is no denial that the workman was paid salary 
by respondent no.2 (contractor). However, from the agreement dated 05.07.2018 (Ex.R-2) placed on file by 
respondent no.1, it emerges that safai karamcharis were provided by respondent no.2 (contractor) to work with 
respondent 10.1. Thus, workman was employee of respondent no.2 and not of respondent 10.1 as has been discussed 
above. There does not exist any relationship of employee and employer between the workman and respondent 10.1. 
However, there exists relation of employee and employer between the workman and respondent 10.2. 


20. Admittedly, there is non-compliance of Section 25F of the Act by respondent no.2. However, as regards 
violation of other provisions i.e. Section 25G and 25H of the Act, there is no evidence lead by the workman. Hence, 
workman is entitled for compensation from respondent no.2. 


21. It is also added here that there is no iota of evidence that any unfair labour practice used by respondent no.1 
by entering into contract with contractors for supply of safai karamcharis and agreement executed between

respondent 10.1 and 2 cannot be said to be any unfair labour practice. So far as contentions of AR for workman that 
the work performed by the workman is of perennial in nature and no domestic inquiry was held before terminating 
the services of workman are concerned, in this regard, it is pointed out that workman was entitled only for 
compensation under Section 25F of the Act by respondent no.2 (contractor) and no domestic inquiry was required to 
be conducted. Merely because work is of perennial in nature does not mean that any right has accrued in favour of the 
workman to get employment with respondent no.1, which is a department of Civil Defence run by Government of 
India and for that regular recruitment procedure is provided. Workman cannot seek backdoor entry into service. 
Moreover, workman is not employee of respondent 10.1 being employee of respondent 10.2 (contractor). 


22. In view of above discussion, it is held that since respondent no.2 (contractor) is currently not working with 
respondent 10.1, so keeping in view the tenure of service rendered by the workman and salary given to him during the 
period of his stay with the contractor and non-compliance of Section 25F of the Act, this Tribunal is of the considered 
opinion that workman is entitled for compensation. 


23. Keeping in view the fact and circumstances of the present case, the following scheme of compensation is 

deemed fit by this Tribunal: 

1. Workman who worked for less than 2 years with contractor shall be entitled for Rs.20,000/-. 

il. Workman who worked for more than 2 years but less than 5 years with contractor shall be entitled 
Rs.30,000/-. 

ili. Workman who worked for more than 5 years with contractors shall be entitled for Rs.50,000/-. 

24. Present workman employed on 09.09.2012 and was terminated on 27.10.2018 (more than 5 years), so he is 

entitled for Rs.50,000/-. 

25. Respondent no.2 is directed to pay the workman Rs.50,000/- within one month from the date of the 


notification of the award failing which the respondent 10.2 shall further pay interest @6% per annum from the date of 
award till the date of making payment. It is also added here that in case respondent 10.1 requires safai karamcharis, 
then workman may be engaged through any contractor on sympathetic ground.

Act.

above ruling, in my considered opinion the applicant herein admittedly falls within the definition of ‘workman’ under 
Section 2(s) of the Act. 


14. The Hon’ble Supreme Court after analyzing the catena of cases has laid down in Balwant Raj Saluja Vs. Air 
India Limited in Civil Appeal No.10266 dated 25.08.2014, two well recognized tests to find out whether the labours 
are the contract employees of the principal employer are:- 


1) Whether the principal employer pays the salary instead of contractor and 


2) Whether the principal employer controls and supervise the work of the employees? 


1090 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : MARCHY 7, 2026/PHALGUNA 16, 1947 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 


15. The facts regarding the payment of salary by the management or contractor has not been stated in the claim 
petition of the workman. In fact, claim petition is totally silent regarding the payment of wages, salary, letter of 
appointment by respondent 10.1 or by contractor or anything likewise. Thus, this basic feature for holding the 
relationship of employer and employee i.e. between respondent 10.1 and workman totally lacking not in the pleading 
but also in the evidence submitted by the workman. However, MW1 Colonel K P Singh in his cross examination has 
stated that it is responsibility of the contractor to pay monthly wages to the conservancy staff provided by him. 
Respondent 10.1 has nothing to do with the minimum wages, DC rate to the conservancy staff. Contractor is 
responsible to give notice to the conservancy staff provided by him. Respondent 10.1 has no roll in terminating the 
services of the workman. Thus, it was the respondent no.2 who was required to ensure the payment of wages to the 
workers engaged by him from time to time. 


16. It is also added here that respondent 10.1 has also placed on record documents Ex.R-1 to Ex.R-4. Ex.R-2 is 
the contract agreement between respondent no.1 & 2. Thus, from the adduced evidence, it emerges that workman was 
paid salary by the contractor and he was being controlled and supervised by the contractor. Thus, there does not exist 
any relationship of employee and employer between the workman and respondent 10.1. However, there exists relation 
of employee and employer between the workman and respondent 10.2. 


17. It is also added here that as per definition of contractor as given in the Section 2(c) of the Contract Labour 
(Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970 (hereinafter called as Contract Act), respondent no.2 was supplying contract 
labour to the respondent 10.1. Thus, respondent no.2 would fall under the definition of contractor. Section 2(c) of the 
Contract Act is reproduced as under: 


“Contractor”, in relation to an establishment, means a person who undertakes to produce a given result for the 
establishment, other than a mere supply of goods or articles of manufacture to such establishment, through contract 
labour or who supplies contract labour for any work of the establishment and includes a sub-contractor; 


18. The Hon’ble Apex Court in the case of Banglore Water Supply & Sewerage Board Vs. A. Rajappa 
1978(36) FLR 266 dealt at length with the ambit and scope of expression “industry” as defined in Section 2(j) of the 


Act, and has laid down triple test for determining whether a particular establishment is industry or not. The triple test 
is where (a) systematic activity (b) organized by cooperation between employer and employee (the direct and 
substantial element is commercial (c) for the production or distribution of goods and services to calculated to satisfy 
human wants and wishes prima facie is an “Industry” in that enterprise. The workman was doing work i.e. systematic 
activity for respondent no.1 at the asking of respondent no.2 and there was cooperation between the workman and 
respondent no.2, which involve substantial commercial element for rendering service to satisfy human wants. Thus, 
respondent no.2 would be termed as industry. 


19. Workman in his deposition has clearly stated that there was non-compliance of Section 25F, 25G and 25H of 
the Act. He also stated that he was appointed on 18.02.2018 and he was paid minimum wages prescribed by Central 
Government and was working with respondent 10.1. He was not given any compensation before terminating his 
services on 27.10.2018. In his cross examination, he has further stated that his salary used to be credited in his bank 
account. But he has not placed on record any bank account, in which his salary was credited in order to enable this 
Court to see who was making payment to the workman. However, there is no denial that the workman was paid salary 
by respondent no.2 (contractor). However, from the agreement dated 05.07.2018 (Ex.R-2) placed on file by 
respondent no.1, it emerges that safai karamcharis were provided by respondent no.2 (contractor) to work with 
respondent no.1. Thus, workman was employee of respondent no.2 and not of respondent no.1 as has been discussed 
above. There does not exist any relationship of employee and employer between the workman and respondent no.1. 
However, there exists relation of employee and employer between the workman and respondent no.2. 


20. Admittedly, there is non-compliance of Section 25F of the Act by respondent no.2. However, as regards 
violation of other provisions i.e. Section 25G and 25H of the Act, there is no evidence lead by the workman. Hence, 
workman is entitled for compensation from respondent no.2. 


21. It is also added here that there is no iota of evidence that any unfair labour practice used by respondent no.1 
by entering into contract with contractors for supply of safai karamcharis and agreement executed between 
respondent 10.1 and 2 cannot be said to be any unfair labour practice. So far as contentions of AR for workman that 
the work performed by the workman is of perennial in nature and no domestic inquiry was held before terminating 
the services of workman are concerned, in this regard, it is pointed out that workman was entitled only for 
compensation under Section 25F of the Act by respondent no.2 (contractor) and no domestic inquiry was required to 
be conducted. Merely because work is of perennial in nature does not mean that any right has accrued in favour of the 
workman to get employment with respondent no.1, which is a department of Civil Defence run by Government of 
India and for that regular recruitment procedure is provided. Workman cannot seek backdoor entry into service. 
Moreover, workman is not employee of respondent 10.1 being employee of respondent no.2 (contractor). 


22. In view of above discussion, it is held that since respondent no.2 (contractor) is currently not working with 
respondent 10.1, so keeping in view the tenure of service rendered by the workman and salary given to him during the 
period of his stay with the contractor and non-compliance of Section 25F of the Act, this Tribunal is of the considered 
opinion that workman is entitled for compensation.

il. Workman who worked for more than 2 years but less than 5 years with contractor shall be entitled 
Rs.30,000/-. 
ili. Workman who worked for more than 5 years with contractors shall be entitled for Rs.50,000/-.

entitled for Rs.20,000/-.

then workman may be engaged through any contractor on sympathetic ground.

13. The first contention regarding the applicant is that whether applicant comes within the definition of

administrative duties. While interpreting Section 2(s) Hon’ble Supreme Court in the case of Devinder Singh Vs. 
Municipal Council, Sanaur, AIR 2011 Supreme Court 2532,has observed as follows:- 


“The source of employment, the quantum of recruitment, the terms & conditions of employment contract of 
service, the quantum of wages/ pay and mode of payment are not at all relevant for deciding whether or not a 
person is a workman within the meaning of Section 2(s) of the Act. The definition of workman also does not 
make any distinction between full time and part time employee or a person appointed on contract basis. 
There is nothing in the plain language of Section 2(s) from which it can be inferred that only person 
employed on regular basis or a person employed for doing whole time job is a workman and the one 
employed on temporary, part time or contract basis on fixed wages or as a casual employee or for doing duty 
for fixed hours is not a workman.” 


14. Thus Hon’ble Supreme Court has clarified that the definition of workman also does not make any distinction 
between full time or part time employee or a person appointed on contract basis. There is nothing in plain language of 
Section 2(s) from which it can be infer that only person employed on regular basis or a person employed for doing 
whole time job is a workman and the one employed on temporary, part time or contract basis on fixed wages or as a 
casual employee or for doing duty for fixed hours is not a workman. In view of the ratio of law enunciated in the 
above ruling, in my considered opinion the applicant herein admittedly falls within the definition of ‘workman’ under 
Section 2(s) of the Act.

12. I have given due consideration to the arguments advanced by AR for both the parties. 


Findings:- 

13. The first contention regarding the applicant is that whether applicant comes within the definition of 
workman as is defined in Section 2(s) of the Act. I may mention that applicant was appointed as sweeper as per his 
claim petition and affidavit submitted before the Tribunal. In plain words the applicant was performing his duties as 
labourer/unskilled worker. He was not in supervisory or administrative post requiring him to perform only 
administrative duties. While interpreting Section 2(s) Hon’ble Supreme Court in the case of Devinder Singh Vs. 
Municipal Council, Sanaur, AIR 2011 Supreme Court 2532,has observed as follows:- 


“The source of employment, the quantum of recruitment, the terms & conditions of employment contract of 
service, the quantum of wages/ pay and mode of payment are not at all relevant for deciding whether or not a 
person is a workman within the meaning of Section 2(s) of the Act. The definition of workman also does not 
make any distinction between full time and part time employee or a person appointed on contract basis. 
There is nothing in the plain language of Section 2(s) from which it can be inferred that only person 
employed on regular basis or a person employed for doing whole time job is a workman and the one 
employed on temporary, part time or contract basis on fixed wages or as a casual employee or for doing duty 
for fixed hours is not a workman.” 


14. Thus Hon’ble Supreme Court has clarified that the definition of workman also does not make any distinction 
between full time or part time employee or a person appointed on contract basis. There is nothing in plain language of 
Section 2(s) from which it can be infer that only person employed on regular basis or a person employed for doing 
whole time job is a workman and the one employed on temporary, part time or contract basis on fixed wages or as a 
casual employee or for doing duty for fixed hours is not a workman. In view of the ratio of law enunciated in the 
above ruling, in my considered opinion the applicant herein admittedly falls within the definition of ‘workman’ under 
Section 2(s) of the Act. 


15. The Hon’ble Supreme Court after analyzing the catena of cases has laid down in Balwant Raj Saluja Vs. Air 
India Limited in Civil Appeal No.10266 dated 25.08.2014, two well recognized tests to find out whether the labours 
are the contract employees of the principal employer are:- 


1) Whether the principal employer pays the salary instead of contractor and 
2) Whether the principal employer controls and supervise the work of the employees? 


16. The facts regarding the payment of salary by the management or contractor has not been stated in the claim 
petition of the workman. In fact, claim petition is totally silent regarding the payment of wages, salary, letter of 
appointment by respondent 10.1 or by contractor or anything likewise. Thus, this basic feature for holding the 
relationship of employer and employee i.e. between respondent 10.1 and workman totally lacking not in the pleading 
but also in the evidence submitted by the workman.However, MW1 Colonel K P Singh in his cross examination has 
stated that it is responsibility of the contractor to pay monthly wages to the conservancy staff provided by him. 
Respondent 10.1 has nothing to do with the minimum wages, DC rate to the conservancy staff. Contractor is 
responsible to give notice to the conservancy staff provided by him. Respondent 10.1 has no roll in terminating the 
services of the workman. Thus, it was the respondent no.2 who was required to ensure the payment of wages to the 
workers engaged by him from time to time. 


17. It is also added here that respondent no.1 has also placed on record documents Ex.R-1 to Ex.R-4. Ex.R-2 is 
the contract agreement between respondent no.1 & 2. Thus, from the adduced evidence, it emerges that workman was

paid salary by the contractor and he was being controlled and supervised by the contractor. Thus, there does not exist 
any relationship of employee and employer between the workman and respondent 10.1. However, there exists relation 
of employee and employer between the workman and respondent no.2. 


18. It is also added here that as per definition of contractor as given in the Section 2(c) of the Contract Labour 
(Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970 (hereinafter called as Contract Act), respondent no.2 was supplying contract 
labour to the respondent 10.1. Thus, respondent 10.2 would fall under the definition of contractor. Section 2(c) of the 
Contract Act is reproduced as under: 


“Contractor”, in relation to an establishment, means a person who undertakes to produce a given result for the 
establishment, other than a mere supply of goods or articles of manufacture to such establishment, through contract 
labour or who supplies contract labour for any work of the establishment and includes a sub-contractor; 


19. Hon’ble Apex Court in the case of Banglore Water Supply & Sewerage Board Vs. A. Rajappa 1978(36) 


FLR 266 dealt at length with the ambit and scope of expression “industry” as defined in Section 2(j) of the Act, and 
has laid down triple test for determining whether a particular establishment is industry or not. The triple test is where 
(a) systematic activity (b) organized by cooperation between employer and employee (the direct and substantial 
element is commercial (c) for the production or distribution of goods and services to calculated to satisfy human 
wants and wishes prima facie is an “Industry” in that enterprise. The workman was doing work i.e. systematic activity 
for respondent 10.1 at the asking of respondent 10.2 and there was cooperation between the workman and respondent 
no.2, which involve substantial commercial element for rendering service to satisfy human wants. Thus, respondent 
no.2 would be termed as industry. 


20. Workman in his deposition has clearly stated that there was non-compliance of Section 25F, 25G and 25H of 
the Act. He also stated that he was appointed on 16.08.2017 and he was paid minimum wages prescribed by Central 
Government and was working with respondent 10.1. He was not given any compensation before terminating his 
services on 27.10.2018. In his cross examination, he has further stated that his salary used to be credited in his bank 
account. But he has not placed on record any bank account, in which his salary was credited in order to enable this 
Court to see who was making payment to the workman. However, there is no denial that the workman was paid salary 
by respondent no.2 (contractor). However, from the agreement dated 05.07.2018 (Ex.R-2) placed on file by 
respondent no.1, it emerges that safai karamcharis were provided by respondent no.2 (contractor) to work with 
respondent 10.1. Thus, workman was employee of respondent 10.2 and not of respondent 10.1 as has been discussed 
above. There does not exist any relationship of employee and employer between the workman and respondent 10.1. 
However, there exists relation of employee and employer between the workman and respondent 10.2. 


21. Admittedly, there is non-compliance of Section 25F of the Act by respondent no.2. However, as regards 
violation of other provisions i.e. Section 25G and 25H of the Act, there is no evidence lead by the workman. Hence, 
workman is entitled for compensation from respondent no.2. 


22. It is also added here that there is no iota of evidence that any unfair labour practice used by respondent no.1 
by entering into contract with contractors for supply of safai karamcharis and agreement executed between 
respondent 10.1 and 2 cannot be said to be any unfair labour practice. So far as contentions of AR for workman that 
the work performed by the workman is of perennial in nature and no domestic inquiry was held before terminating 
the services of workman are concerned, in this regard, it is pointed out that workman was entitled only for 
compensation under Section 25F of the Act by respondent no.2 (contractor) and no domestic inquiry was required to 
be conducted. Merely because work is of perennial in nature does not mean that any right has accrued in favour of the 
workman to get employment with respondent no.1, which is a department of Civil Defence run by Government of 
India and for that regular recruitment procedure is provided. Workman cannot seek backdoor entry into service. 
Moreover, workman is not employee of respondent 10.1 being employee of respondent no.2 (contractor). 


23. In view of above discussion, it is held that since respondent no.2 (contractor) is currently not working with 
respondent 10.1, so keeping in view the tenure of service rendered by the workman and salary given to him during the 
period of his stay with the contractor and non-compliance of Section 25F of the Act, this Tribunal is of the considered 
opinion that workman is entitled for compensation. 


24. Keeping in view the fact and circumstances of the present case, the following scheme of compensation is 
deemed fit by this Tribunal: 


1. Workman who worked for less than 2 years with contractor shall be entitled for Rs.20,000/-. 

il. Workman who worked for more than 2 years but less than 5 years with contractor shall be entitled 
Rs.30,000/-. 

ili. Workman who worked for more than 5 years with contractors shall be entitled for Rs.50,000/-. 


25. Present workman employed on 16.08.2017 and was terminated on 27.10.2018 (less than 2 years), so he is 
entitled for Rs.20,000/-.

18. It is also added here that as per definition of contractor as given in the Section 2(c) of the Contract Labour 
(Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970 (hereinafter called as Contract Act), respondent no.2 was supplying contract 
labour to the respondent no.1. Thus, respondent no.2 would fall under the definition of contractor. Section 2(c) of 
the Contract Act is reproduced as under: 


“Contractor”, in relation to an establishment, means a person who undertakes to produce a given result for the 
establishment, other than a mere supply of goods or articles of manufacture to such establishment, through contract 
labour or who supplies contract labour for any work of the establishment and includes a sub-contractor; 


19. TheHon’ble Apex Court in the case of Banglore Water Supply & Sewerage Board Vs. A. Rajappa 1978(36) 
FLR 266 dealt at length with the ambit and scope of expression “industry” as defined in Section 2(j) of the Act, and 


has laid down triple test for determining whether a particular establishment is industry or not. The triple test is 
where (a) systematic activity (b) organized by cooperation between employer and employee (the direct and 
substantial element is commercial (c) for the production or distribution of goods and services to calculated to satisfy 
human wants and wishes prima facie is an “Industry” in that enterprise. The workman was doing work i.e. 
systematic activity for respondent no.1 at the asking of respondent no.2 and there was cooperation between the 
workman and respondent no.2, which involve substantial commercial element for rendering service to satisfy human 
wants. Thus, respondent no.2 would be termed as industry. 


20. Workman in his deposition has clearly stated that there was non-compliance of Section 25F, 25G and 25H of 
the Act. He also stated that he was appointed on 20.08.2012 and he was paid minimum wages prescribed by Central 
Government and was working with respondent 10.1. He was not given any compensation before terminating his 
services on 27.10.2018. In his cross examination, he has further stated that his salary used to be credited in his bank 
account. But he has not placed on record any bank account, in which his salary was credited in order to enable this 
Court to see who was making payment to the workman. However, there is no denial that the workman was paid 
salary by respondent no.2 (contractor). However, from the agreement dated 05.07.2018 (Ex.R-2) placed on file by 
respondent no.1, it emerges that safai karamcharis were provided by respondent no.2 (contractor) to work with 
respondent 10.1. Thus, workman was employee of respondent 10.2 and not of respondent 10.1 as has been discussed 
above. There does not exist any relationship of employee and employer between the workman and respondent 10.1. 
However, there exists relation of employee and employer between the workman and respondent 10.2. 


21. Admittedly, there is non-compliance of Section 25F of the Act by respondent no.2. However, as regards 
violation of other provisions i.e. Section 25G and 25H of the Act, there is no evidence lead by the workman. Hence, 
workman is entitled for compensation from respondent 10.2. 


22: It is also added here that there is no iota of evidence that any unfair labour practice used by respondent 10.1 
by entering into contract with contractors for supply of safai karamcharis and agreement executed between 
respondent 10.1 and 2 cannot be said to be any unfair labour practice. So far as contentions of AR for workman that 
the work performed by the workman is of perennial in nature and no domestic inquiry was held before terminating 
the services of workman are concerned, in this regard, it is pointed out that workman was entitled only for 
compensation under Section 25F of the Act by respondent no.2 (contractor) and no domestic inquiry was required to 
be conducted. Merely because work is of perennial in nature does not mean that any right has accrued in favour of 
the workman to get employment with respondent no.1, which is a department of Civil Defence run by Government 
of India and for that regular recruitment procedure is provided. Workman cannot seek backdoor entry into service. 
Moreover, workman is not employee of respondent 10.1 being employee of respondent 10.2 (contractor). 


23. In view of above discussion, it is held that since respondent no.2 (contractor) is currently not working with 
respondent no.1, so keeping in view the tenure of service rendered by the workman and salary given to him during 
the period of his stay with the contractor and non-compliance of Section 25F of the Act, this Tribunal is of the 
considered opinion that workman is entitled for compensation. 

24. Keeping in view the fact and circumstances of the present case, the following scheme of compensation is 
deemed fit by this Tribunal: 

1. Workman who worked for less than 2 years with contractor shall be entitled for Rs.20,000/-. 


ii. | Workman who worked for more than 2 years but less than 5 years with contractor shall be entitled 


Rs.30,000/-. 
ili. Workman who worked for more than 5 years with contractors shall be entitled for Rs.50,000/-. 
25. Present workman employed on 20.08.2012 and was terminated on 27.10.2018 (more than 5 years), so he is 
entitled for Rs.50,000/-. 
26. Respondent no.2 is directed to pay the workman Rs.50,000/- within one month from the date of the 


notification of the award failing which the respondent no.2 shall further pay interest @6% per annum from the date 
of award till the date of making payment. It is also added here that in case respondent 10.1 requires safai 
karamcharis, then workman may be engaged through any contractor on sympathetic ground. 


27. Let copy of this award be sent to Central Government for publication as required under Section 17 of 
the Act.

Respondent No.1 has admitted that the Petitioner had worked in the work of Strapping Mills Products WRM in its

Respondent or 3" Respondent. However, Respondent has filed photocopies of documents as proof of payment to the 
workman by R-2. The perusal of these photocopies goes to show that these are not proved by any cogent and relevant 
evidence of witness. Therefore, these photocopies in respect of payment are not admissible in evidence. Moreover, 
the genuineness of these document photocopies has been challenged by the Petitioner in his rejoinder, therefore, 
burden of proof to prove the factum of payment to the Petitioner lies on the Respondent No.1 which he failed to 
discharge. Thus, it is established that Petitioner is entitled to receive the amount towards benefits upon his 
retrenchment from service by R-3. Moreover, Respondent No.1 is the Principal Employer of Petitioner contract 
labour, therefore, Respondent No.1 is also liable to pay retrenchment allowances to Petitioner along with Respondent

15. In this context, relevant decisions of the Hon’ble Supreme Court and High Court, are discussed as 
hereunder: - 


(a) In the case of Sail Growth Works versus Nilmani Lal and others, Writ Petition Number 386 of 2025, dated 
107 March 2025, the Hon’ble High Court of Kolkata has held: 


19. Gratuity, payable under the Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972, is a gratuitous payment required to be 
made by an employer to his employee at the time of termination of services of the employee or upon such 
employee’s death. 


Section 21 (4) of the Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970 (CLRA), mandates that a 
principal employer is responsible for the payment of 'wages' to a contract employee in the event of a contractor's 
failure to pay within the stipulated timelines or in the event of a contractor making a short payment. The principal 
employer then has the ability to recover the amount paid as 'wages', from the contractor. Section 2(h) of the CLRA 
defines the term 'wages' as all remuneration (whether by salary, allowances or otherwise) expressed in terms of 
money or capable of being so expressed, which would if the terms of employment, expressed or implied, were 
fulfilled, be payable to a person employed in respect of his employment or of work done in such employment and 
includes, among others, ''(d) any sum which by reason of the termination of employment of the person employed is 
payable under any law, contract or instrument which provides for the payment..."". However, it excludes (6) any 
gratuity payable on the termination of employees in cases other than those specified in (d)."" In Superintending 
Engineer, Mettur Thermal Power Station, Mettur vs. Appellate Page 11 Authority, Joint Commissioner of Labour, 
Coimbatore & Anr, 2012 LLR 1160, it has been held by the Madras High Court that gratuity payable under the 
Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972 falls within this definition of 'wages'. The principal employer or the contractor may 
be liable to pay gratuity to contract employees, depending on the circumstances. Principal employer The principal 
employer is liable to pay gratuity to contract employees if the contractor fails to pay. The principal employer is 
liable to pay gratuity if the contractor makes a short payment. 


The principal employer is liable to pay gratuity if the contractor terminates the services of the contract 
employee. The principal employer is liable to pay gratuity if the contract employee works for multiple contractors.

Contractor The contractor is liable to pay gratuity to contract employees if they have worked for at least five years 
and the contract is separate from the company. 


(b) In the case of Hindustan Steel Works Construction Limited versus Commissioner of Labour, Appeal Civil 
Number 11355 of 1996, dated 37 September 1996, the Hon’ble Court have held: - 


“The short question that arises for determination is whether the appellant who the principal employer is 
liable to pay to the contract workers any amount which constitutes the difference between the wages payable 
to the contract labour by the contractor and the wages paid by the appellant to its own employees doing 
similar work. The Division Bench seems to have relied upon Section 21(4) of the said Act for this purpose. 
Section 21(1), however, provides that the contractor shall be responsible for the payment of wages to each 
worker employed by his. Section 21(4) provides that if the contractor fails to make this payment or any part 
thereof, the principal employer is liable to make this payment and may recover the same from the contractor 
as set out in that sub-section. Looking to the definition of wages Under the said Act read with the definition 
of wages in the payment of Wages Act, which we have set out earlier, it is clear that Section 21 only deals 
with the payment of contractual wages by the contractor to each of his worker; The definition of wages 
would cover within its scope, inter alia, also those amounts which the contractor is liable to pay his workers 
under any award, settlement or order of court as well as other amounts falling within the definition of wages 
under the payment of Wages Act Subjection (2) provides for a representative of the principal employer 
supervising this payment. Clearly, therefore, the wages which are the subject-matter of Section 21 are 
specified sums which are payable in present by the contractor under the terms of his contract of employment 
with each worker as well as under any existing award, settlement or order of the court. -Section 21 does not 
deal with, nor does if cover the Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Rules, 1971. Hence Section 
21(4) will not apply to such obligations of the contractor which may be the subject-matter of dispute between 
the contractor and his workers at time of disbursement of wages and which do not fall within the definition 
of “wages” under the Act.” 


(c) Further, Hon’ble Supreme Court in the case of M/s. Bombay Industries Chemical Industries Vs Deputy 
Labour Commissioner, Civil Appeal Number 813 of 2022, D.O.D dated 4" February 2022, the Hon’ble Supreme 
Court has held that the benefit sought to be enforced under Section 33C (2) of the ID Act is necessarily a pre-existing 
benefit or one flowing from a pre-existing right. The Hon’ble Court added that in the case of Kanku Ben, it is 
observed and held that whenever a workman is entitled to receive from his employer any money or any benefit which 
is capable of being computed in terms of money and which he is entitled to receive from his employer and is denied 
of such benefit can approach Labour Court Under section 33-C(2) of the ID Act. It is further observed that the benefit 
sought to be enforced Under Section 33C (2) of the ID Act is necessarily a preexisting benefit or one flowing from a 
preexisting right. The difference between a preexisting right or benefit on one hand and the right or benefit, which is 
considered just and fair on the other hand is vital. The former falls within jurisdiction of Labour Court exercising 
powers under Section 33C (2) of the ID Act, while the latter does not. 


(d) In the case of Jeet Lal Sharma versus Presiding Officer, 2001 VAD Delhi One, dated 157 March 2000, the 
Hon’ble High Court of Delhi have held:- 


“15. The point which is emphasised is that entitlement to receive money the pre-existing right can the 
based on (1) adjudication (2) settlement (3) service conditions. If the right to get a particular benefit is there, the 
application us. 13-C(2) would be maintainable and jurisdiction of Labour Court will not be barred merely because 
employer has denied the same 


16. What is the meaning of the expression "entitlement in receive". No doubt it is referable to pre-existing 
right. However where the workman claims a benefit flowing from a pre-existing right and approaches the Labour 
Courts 33-612) for computation of the right in term of money and the employer disputes the existences of the right, 
the Labour Court will have the jurisdiction to determine the question, whether the right exists and if the existence 
of right is established than in proceed in compute the benefit flowing therefrom in terms of money or on its 
decisions recovery proceedings start (New Taj Mahal Cafe Private Limited versus Labour Court reported in 1970 
(2) LLN 51 and East India Coal Company Limited (supra) In deciding the maintainability of the application u/s 
13-(12) what is in be looked at is the clans set up in the application and not what the other side contends in its 
reply. The fact that the employer by his plea rises some dispute, does not mean that Jurisdiction of Labour Court to 
deal with the question is taken away.” 


16. Thus, in view of forgone discussion and law laid down by Hon’ble Court as discussed above, Petition filed by the 
Petitioner under Section 33-C(2) of ID Act,1947 against the Respondents for recovery of retrenchment allowances as 
per Ex. W12 is acceptable. Undisputedly, Petitioner was engaged by Respondent No.3 M/s Rishitha Associates, and 
Respondent No.2 has engaged Respondent No. 3 as sub-contractor for Labour supply to work in the establishment of

Respondent No.2 as main contractor is jointly and severally liable for payment of the claimed amount to the

The definition of retrenchment as provided under Section 2 (00) is extracted as here under: - 


“2(00) “retrenchment “means the termination by the employer f the service of a workman for any reason 
whatsoever, otherwise than as punishment inflicted by way of disciplinary action but does not include---

contained therein; or” 


Although Petitioner might be working with Respondent No.1 even after 15.08.2012 but Respondent No.3 is no more 
employer of workman. Therefore, only conclusion can be drawn in such circumstances that Respondent No. 3 has 
terminated the service of Petitioner w.e.f 16.08.2012. Thus, Petitioner is entitled to receive retrenchment/allowance as 
per Ex. W12. Thus, the contention of R3 in this context is untenable. Therefore, the plea of Petitioner that Petitioner 
worker is working now under new contractor is untenable as the Respondent No. 3 is no more employer of the 
Petitioner after 15-08-2012 meaning thereby Petitioner has been terminated by Respondent No. 3 from service 
w.e.f 16.08.2012 and is entitled to receive retrenchment allowances as per terns of the contract. 


17. | However, Respondent No. 1 has contended that terminal benefits claimed by the Petitioner do not form part of 
wages and as such the contractor as direct employer is responsible to make all other payments. In this context, the 
reference of definition of wages u/s 2 (IV) Payment of Wages Act, 1936 is relevant. Therein it is provided that wages 
mean all remuneration (whether by way of salaries, allowances or otherwise) expressed in terms of money are capable 
of being so expressed which would if the terms of employment, expressed or employed were fulfilled be payable to 
person employed in respect of his employer or of work done in such employer and includes. 


(d) Any sum which by reason of termination of employment of the person employed is payable under any law 
contract or instrument which provides for the payment of such sum whether with nor without deduction but does not 
provide for the time within which the payment is to be made. 


Thus, in view of the above definition of wages the retrenchment allowances are very much covered under the 
definition of wages and the contention of the Respondent No.1 that retrenchment allowances are not included under 
the wages is untenable. According to Ex. W12 the term of payment/mode of payment has been agreed upon between 
Respondent No.2 the main contractor and Respondent No.3 sub-contractor, to be paid to the contract Labour i.e. 
Petitioner for doing the work at Respondent No.1! industry. The employment of Petitioner by Respondent No.3 of the 
Petitioner has been admitted by Respondent No. | & 2 and it is also admitted that retrenchment allowances of the 
Petitioner workman has not been paid by none of the Respondents. Therefore, as a Principal Employer Respondent 
No.1 is liable to pay retrenchment allowance to the Petitioner in view of the provision contained under Section 21 (4) 
of Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970 and he may recover the said amount of retrenchment 
allowances so paid to Petitioner from Respondent No. 2 and Respondent No. 3. Thus, the contention of Respondent 
No. 1 in this context is untenable. 


18. Therefore, in view of foregone discussion and law laid down by Hon’ble Court as discussed in preceding 
paragraph of this order, I come to irresistible conclusion that as per document Ex. W8 and W12 Petitioner had worked 
with the Respondent No. 1 as contract labour employed by Respondent No.3 as sub-contractor of Respondent No.2, 
during the period from 16-08-2009 to 15-08-2012 and Respondent No.3 the employer has terminated the services of 
Petitioner w.e.f 16-08-2012. Therefore, Petitioner is entitled for payment of retrenchment allowances as per 
document Ex. W12 which has been proved by the oral and documentary evidence of Petitioner and also admitted by 
Respondent No. 3 it is undisputed that none of the Respondents has paid such retrenchment allowance to the 
Petitioner. Therefore, as per provision contained under section 21 (4) of contract labour (Regulation and Abolition) 
Act, 1970 the Respondent No. 1 being principal employer is responsible for payment of retrenchment allowance to 
Petitioner, and he may recover said amount paid to Petitioner from Respondent No. 1 and 2 jointly and severally. 
Thus, the Petition filed by the Petitioner has merits and deserved to be allowed.

11. Perused the record. At the outset, Respondent counsel urged that present petition filed by the Petitioner for the 
recovery of full and final payment amounting to Rs.83,537.85ps. along with the interest for the work under contract is 
not maintainable under section 33-C(2) of ID Act 1947 as there is no amount due to the Petitioner from Respondent. 


Firstly, we have to examine provision contained under section 33 C (2) of the ID Act. Section 33 C (2) of ID Act 
provides :- 


"Where any workman is entitled to receive from the employer any money or any benefit which is capable 
of being computed in terms of money, and if any question arises as to the amount of money due or as to the 
amount at which such benefit should be computed, then the question may, subject to any rules that may be 
wait under this act, be decided by such labour court as may be specified in this behalf by the appropriate 
government within a period of not exceeding three month." 


Thus, in view of provision contained u/s 33-C (2) we proceed to examine the question whether the Petitioner is 
entitled to receive from employer any money or benefit which is capable of being computed in terms of money. 
Petitioner has filed affidavit therein he has disposed that in MP. No. 2/2017 Co-workman has disposed as WWI in 
evidence and exhibited document W1 to W22. The evidence recorded in said petition may be treated as evidence of 
Petitioner in this case including cross examination of WW1. Since Petitioner has similar averment and evidence in 
both the petition. It is settled law that the rule of evidence Act do not apply strictly to the matter under I.D. Act. 
Therefore, evidence recorded in MPNo.2-2017 is taken on record and considered in this Petition in support of claim 
of Petitioner. In this context Petitioner has filed documents in evidence 


which has been exhibited by witness WW1.The perusal of these document reveals that the document Ex. W1 is the

against his name the total number of working days 899 has been recorded. Further, document Ex. W15 is the 
statement of full and final amount calculation, and these details has been prepared and signed by the authorized 
signatories of Respondent No.2. This document goes to show that at Sl. No.9 name of the Petitioner, Sri P.V.R. 
Reddy, unskilled workman is recorded and against his name amount due towards full and final amount is shown as 
Rs.83,537.85ps Further, document Ex. W16 is the letter dated 377 December 2013, addressed to the General Manager 
Vishakhapatnam Steel Plant, Respondent No.1 by Respondent No.2 regarding labour benefit payment directly which 
is to be cleared by Respondent No.2 in respect of contract labour for the period from 16" August 2009 to 15" August 
2012. Similarly, documents Ex. W17 and W20 are the letters addressed to Respondent No.1! by Respondent No.2 for 
release of amount equivalent to full and final benefit due to contract labour. Thus, on going oral and documentary 
evidence produced by the Petitioner, it is established that Petitioner was engaged by the Respondent No.3 as contract 
labour for the work of Respondent No.1 on behalf of Respondent No.2 during the period from 12.8.2009 to 12.8.2012 
and he is entitled to receive Rs. 83,537.85ps. towards full and final payment as terminal benefit from Respondent 
No.3 as per terms of contract Ex.W8, W9, and Ex. W12. Further, it is established that Petitioner was engaged for 
work by Respondent No. 3 i.e., Rishitha Associates for the period from 16.8.2009 to 15.8.2012 to work in industry of 
R-1 Principal Employer Rashtriya Ispat Nigam Ltd, Vishakpatnam Steel Plant. 


13. Although Respondent has contended that all the wages and dues towards the final settlement have been paid 
to the Petitioner workman but in support of his contention Respondent has not filed any document to corroborate it. 
Respondent No. | has also examined witness MW2 Sri K. Sudhakar Rao who has produced and exhibited document 
Ex.M1 to Ex.M6 and states that Ex. M6 is showing the amount paid by 20 Respondent to claimants but in cross 
examination MW? states that it is true that Ex.M6 relates to amount Rs. 28,58,522/- which is mentioned in para 5 of 
chief statement of MW1 and he is not aware that Rs. 61,76,628/- is still balance due to be paid to workman. Thus, the 
testimony of MW2 is not direct evidence in respect of payment of claimed amount in the petition, hence his evidence 
is not relevant in this regard. Therefore, contention of the Respondent No.1 in this context is untenable for the want 
of cogent and relevant evidence. Thus, on going oral and documentary evidence on record, it is established that the 
Petitioner workman is entitled to receive from the employer Respondent No.3 the amount of Rs.83,537.85ps. for the 
period of August,2009 to 2012 towards retrenchment allowances as per document Ex. W12.

14. Now, question arises that who is liable to pay the said retrenchment allowances to the Petitioner as per 
contract. Admittedly, Petitioner workman was engaged by Respondent No.3 for the work of Respondent No.1. 
Respondent No.1 has admitted that the Petitioner had worked in the work of Strapping Mills Products WRM in its 
industry during the period from 16.8.2009 to 15.8.2012 as contract labour engaged by Respondent No.3. Since the 
Respondent No. 3 was sub-contractor for labour supply for the work order Ex. W8 of Respondent No.2, therefore, 
Respondent No.1, Respondent No.2 and Respondent No.3 are jointly and severally liable to pay retrenchment 
allowances towards the full and final payment to the Petitioner as per contract. Although Respondent No.3 contended 
that it has paid all the money due to the Petitioner, but Respondent No.3 has not produced any document to establish 
that full and final payment as claimed by the Petitioner towards retrenchment allowances has been paid by 2" 
Respondent or 37 Respondent. However, Respondent has filed photocopies of documents as proof of payment to the 
workman by R-2. The perusal of these photocopies goes to show that these are not proved by any cogent and relevant 
evidence of witness. Therefore, these photocopies in respect of payment are not admissible in evidence. Moreover, 
the genuineness of these document photocopies has been challenged by the Petitioner in his rejoinder, therefore, 
burden of proof to prove the factum of payment to the Petitioner lies on the Respondent No.1 which he failed to 
discharge. Thus, it is established that Petitioner is entitled to receive the amount towards benefits upon his 
retrenchment from service by R-3. Moreover, Respondent No.1 is the Principal Employer of Petitioner contract 
labour, therefore, Respondent No.1 is also liable to pay retrenchment allowances to Petitioner along with Respondent 
No.2 and Respondent No.3 jointly and severally. 


15. In this context, relevant decisions of the Hon’ble Supreme Court and High Court, are discussed as 
hereunder: - 


(a) In the case of Sail Growth Works versus Nilmani Lal and others, Writ Petition Number 386 of 2025, dated 10" 
March 2025, the Hon’ble High Court of Kolkata has held: 


19. Gratuity, payable under the Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972, is a gratuitous payment required to be 
made by an employer to his employee at the time of termination of services of the employee or upon such 
employee’s death. 


Section 21 (4) of the Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970 (CLRA), mandates that a 
principal employer is responsible for the payment of 'wages' to a contract employee in the event of a contractor's 
failure to pay within the stipulated timelines or in the event of a contractor making a short payment. The principal 
employer then has the ability to recover the amount paid as 'wages', from the contractor. Section 2(h) of the CLRA 
defines the term 'wages' as all remuneration (whether by salary, allowances or otherwise) expressed in terms of 
money or capable of being so expressed, which would if the terms of employment, expressed or implied, were 
fulfilled, be payable to a person employed in respect of his employment or of work done in such employment and 
includes, among others, (६) any sum which by reason of the termination of employment of the person employed is 
payable under any law, contract or instrument which provides for the payment..."". However, it excludes (6) any 
gratuity payable on the termination of employees in cases other than those specified in (d)."" In Superintending 
Engineer, Mettur Thermal Power Station, Mettur vs. Appellate Page 11 Authority, Joint Commissioner of Labour, 
Coimbatore & Anr, 2012 LLR 1160, it has been held by the Madras High Court that gratuity payable under the 
Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972 falls within this definition of 'wages'. The principal employer or the contractor may 
be liable to pay gratuity to contract employees, depending on the circumstances. Principal employer The principal 
employer is liable to pay gratuity to contract employees if the contractor fails to pay. The principal employer is 
liable to pay gratuity if the contractor makes a short payment. 


The principal employer is liable to pay gratuity if the contractor terminates the services of the contract 
employee. The principal employer is liable to pay gratuity if the contract employee works for multiple contractors. 
Contractor The contractor is liable to pay gratuity to contract employees if they have worked for at least five years 
and the contract is separate from the company. 


(b) In the case of Hindustan Steel Works Construction Limited versus Commissioner of Labour, Appeal Civil 
Number 11355 of 1996, dated 37 September 1996, the Hon’ble Court have held: - 


“The short question that arises for determination is whether the appellant who the principal employer is 
liable to pay to the contract workers any amount which constitutes the difference between the wages payable 
to the contract labour by the contractor and the wages paid by the appellant to its own employees doing 
similar work. The Division Bench seems to have relied upon Section 21(4) of the said Act for this purpose. 
Section 21(1), however, provides that the contractor shall be responsible for the payment of wages to each 
worker employed by his. Section 21(4) provides that if the contractor fails to make this payment or any part 
thereof, the principal employer is liable to make this payment and may recover the same from the contractor 
as set out in that sub-section. Looking to the definition of wages Under the said Act read with the definition 
of wages in the payment of Wages Act, which we have set out earlier, it is clear that Section 21 only deals 
with the payment of contractual wages by the contractor to each of his worker; The definition of wages 
would cover within its scope, inter alia, also those amounts which the contractor is liable to pay his workers

under any award, settlement or order of court as well as other amounts falling within the definition of wages 
under the payment of Wages Act Subjection (2) provides for a representative of the principal employer 
supervising this payment. Clearly, therefore, the wages which are the subject-matter of Section 21 are 
specified sums which are payable in present by the contractor under the terms of his contract of employment 
with each worker as well as under any existing award, settlement or order of the court. -Section 21 does not 
deal with, nor does if cover the Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Rules, 1971. Hence Section 
21(4) will not apply to such obligations of the contractor which may be the subject-matter of dispute between 
the contractor and his workers at time of disbursement of wages and which do not fall within the definition 
of “wages” under the Act.” 


(c) Further, Hon’ble Supreme Court in the case of M/s. Bombay Industries Chemical Industries Vs Deputy 
Labour Commissioner, Civil Appeal Number 813 of 2022, D.O.D dated 4" February 2022, the Hon’ble Supreme 
Court has held that the benefit sought to be enforced under Section 33C (2) of the ID Act is necessarily a pre-existing 
benefit or one flowing from a pre-existing right. The Hon’ble Court added that in the case of Kanku Ben, it is 
observed and held that whenever a workman is entitled to receive from his employer any money or any benefit which 
is capable of being computed in terms of money and which he is entitled to receive from his employer and is denied 
of such benefit can approach Labour Court Under section 33-C(2) of the ID Act. It is further observed that the benefit 
sought to be enforced Under Section 33C (2) of the ID Act is necessarily a preexisting benefit or one flowing from a 
preexisting right. The difference between a preexisting right or benefit on one hand and the right or benefit, which is 
considered just and fair on the other hand is vital. The former falls within jurisdiction of Labour Court exercising 
powers under Section 33C (2) of the ID Act, while the latter does not. 


(d) In the case of Jeet Lal Sharma versus Presiding Officer, 2001 VAD Delhi One, dated 157 March 2000, the 
Hon’ble High Court of Delhi have held:- 


“15. The point which is emphasised is that entitlement to receive money the pre-existing right can the 
based on (1) adjudication (2) settlement (3) service conditions. If the right to get a particular benefit is there, the 
application us. 13-C(2) would be maintainable and jurisdiction of Labour Court will not be barred merely because 
employer has denied the same 


16. What is the meaning of the expression "entitlement in receive". No doubt it is referable to pre-existing 
right. However where the workman claims a benefit flowing from a pre-existing right and approaches the Labour 
Courts 33-612) for computation of the right in term of money and the employer disputes the existences of the right, 
the Labour Court will have the jurisdiction to determine the question, whether the right exists and if the existence 
of right is established than in proceed in compute the benefit flowing therefrom in terms of money or on its 
decisions recovery proceedings start (New Taj Mahal Cafe Private Limited versus Labour Court reported in 1970 
(2) LLN 51 and East India Coal Company Limited (supra) In deciding the maintainability of the application u/s 
13-(12) what is in be looked at is the clans set up in the application and not what the other side contends in its 
reply. The fact that the employer by his plea rises some dispute, does not mean that Jurisdiction of Labour Court to 
deal with the question is taken away.” 


16. Thus, in view of forgone discussion and law laid down by Hon’ble Court as discussed above, Petition filed by the 
Petitioner under Section 33-C(2) of ID Act,1947 against the Respondents for recovery of retrenchment allowances as 
per Ex. W12 is acceptable. Undisputedly, Petitioner was engaged by Respondent No.3 M/s Rishitha Associates, and 
Respondent No.2 has engaged Respondent No. 3 as sub-contractor for Labour supply to work in the establishment of 
Respondent No.1 with prior approval vide document Ex. W8. Therefore, Respondent No.3 as such contractor for 
Labour supply for the work is responsible for payment of retrenchment allowances to the Petitioner. It has come on 
record Respondent No.3 has not paid the claimed amount to the Petitioner. Therefore, Respondent No. 3 and 
Respondent No.2 as main contractor is jointly and severally liable for payment of the claimed amount to the 
Petitioner. However, Respondent No.3 has contended that the Petitioner has not been retrenched by him and 
Petitioner is still continuing work with the Respondent No.1 under new contractor. Therefore, Petitioner is not entitled 
to recover retrenchment allowances from Respondent. Undisputedly, Petitioner was engaged by Respondent No.3 to 
work in the establishment of Respondent No.1 for the period from 16.08.2009 to 15.08.2012 as per Ex. W8. 
Respondent No.3 is no more employer of Petitioner after 15.08.2012 of the petitioner w.e.f 16-08-2012 and it makes 
no difference whether petitioner is still working with Respondent No.1 under some other contention. Thus, 
Respondent No.3 has retrenched services of Petitioner w.e.f 16.08.2012. 


The definition of retrenchment as provided under Section 2 (00) is extracted as here under: - 


“2(00) “retrenchment “means the termination by the employer f the service of a workman for any reason 
whatsoever, otherwise than as punishment inflicted by way of disciplinary action but does not include--- 


(a) Voluntary retirement of the workman: or 


(b) Retirement of the workman on reaching the age of superannuation if the contract 
of employment between the employer and the workman concerned contains a 
stipulation in that behalf; or

(bb) termination of the service of the workman as a result of the non-renewal of the 
contract of employment between the employer and the stipulation in that behalf 
contained therein; or” 


Although Petitioner might be working with Respondent No.1 even after 15.08.2012 but Respondent No.3 is no more 
employer of workman. Therefore, only conclusion can be drawn in such circumstances that Respondent No. 3 has 
terminated the service of Petitioner w.e.f 16.08.2012. Thus, Petitioner is entitled to receive retrenchment/allowance as 
per Ex. W12. Thus, the contention of R3 in this context is untenable. Therefore, the plea of Petitioner that Petitioner 
worker is working now under new contractor is untenable as the Respondent No. 3 is no more employer of the 
Petitioner after 15-08-2012 meaning thereby Petitioner has been terminated by Respondent No. 3 from service w.e.f 
16.08.2012 and is entitled to receive retrenchment allowances as per terns of the contract. 


17. | However, Respondent No. 1 has contended that terminal benefits claimed by the Petitioner do not form part of 
wages and as such the contractor as direct employer is responsible to make all other payments. In this context, the 
reference of definition of wages u/s 2 (IV) Payment of Wages Act, 1936 is relevant. Therein it is provided that wages 
mean all remuneration (whether by way of salaries, allowances or otherwise) expressed in terms of money are capable 
of being so expressed which would if the terms of employment, expressed or employed were fulfilled be payable to 
person employed in respect of his employer or of work done in such employer and includes. 


(d) Any sum which by reason of termination of employment of the person employed is payable under any law 
contract or instrument which provides for the payment of such sum whether with nor without deduction but does not 
provide for the time within which the payment is to be made. 


Thus, in view of the above definition of wages the retrenchment allowances are very much covered under the 
definition of wages and the contention of the Respondent No.1 that retrenchment allowances are not included under 
the wages is untenable. According to Ex. W12 the term of payment/mode of payment has been agreed upon between 
Respondent No.2 the main contractor and Respondent No.3 sub-contractor, to be paid to the contract Labour i.e. 
Petitioner for doing the work at Respondent No.1! industry. The employment of Petitioner by Respondent No.3 of the 
Petitioner has been admitted by Respondent No. | & 2 and it is also admitted that retrenchment allowances of the 
Petitioner workman has not been paid by none of the Respondents. Therefore, as a Principal Employer Respondent 
No.1 is liable to pay retrenchment allowance to the Petitioner in view of the provision contained under Section 21 (4) 
of Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970 and he may recover the said amount of retrenchment 
allowances so paid to Petitioner from Respondent No. 2 and Respondent No. 3. Thus, the contention of Respondent 
No. | in this context is untenable. 


18. Therefore, in view of foregone discussion and law laid down by Hon’ble Court as discussed in preceding 
paragraph of this order, I come to irresistible conclusion that as per document Ex. W8 and W12 Petitioner had worked 
with the Respondent No. 1 as contract labour employed by Respondent No.3 as sub-contractor of Respondent No.2, 
during the period from 16-08-2009 to 15-08-2012 and Respondent No.3 the employer has terminated the services of 
Petitioner w.e.f 16-08-2012. Therefore, Petitioner is entitled for payment of retrenchment allowances as per 
document Ex. W12 which has been proved by the oral and documentary evidence of Petitioner and also admitted by 
Respondent No. 3 it is undisputed that none of the Respondents has paid such retrenchment allowance to the 
Petitioner. Therefore, as per provision contained under section 21 (4) of contract labour (Regulation and Abolition) 
Act, 1970 the Respondent No. 1 being principal employer is responsible for payment of retrenchment allowance to 
Petitioner, and he may recover said amount paid to Petitioner from Respondent No. 1 and 2 jointly and severally. 
Thus, the Petition filed by the Petitioner has merits and deserved to be allowed. 


ORDER 


The Petition filed by the Petitioner under section 33C(2) of ID Act 1947 corresponding section 59 (2) under 
the Industrial Relation Code is allowed. 


Respondent No. 1 Chairman & Managing Director, Rastriya Ispat Nigam Ltd, Visakhapatnam Steel Plant,

15. In this context, relevant decisions of the Hon’ble Supreme Court and High Court, are discussed as 
hereunder: - 


(a) In the case of Sail Growth Works versus Nilmani Lal and others, Writ Petition Number 386 of 2025, dated 10" 
March 2025, the Hon’ble High Court of Kolkata has held: 


19. Gratuity, payable under the Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972, is a gratuitous payment required to be 
made by an employer to his employee at the time of termination of services of the employee or upon such 
employee’s death. 


Section 21 (4) of the Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970 (CLRA), mandates that a 
principal employer is responsible for the payment of 'wages' to a contract employee in the event of a contractor's 
failure to pay within the stipulated timelines or in the event of a contractor making a short payment. The principal 
employer then has the ability to recover the amount paid as 'wages', from the contractor. Section 2(h) of the CLRA 
defines the term 'wages' as all remuneration (whether by salary, allowances or otherwise) expressed in terms of 
money or capable of being so expressed, which would if the terms of employment, expressed or implied, were 
fulfilled, be payable to a person employed in respect of his employment or of work done in such employment and 
includes, among others, ''(d) any sum which by reason of the termination of employment of the person employed is 
payable under any law, contract or instrument which provides for the payment..."". However, it excludes (6) any 
gratuity payable on the termination of employees in cases other than those specified in (d)."" In Superintending 
Engineer, Mettur Thermal Power Station, Mettur vs. Appellate Page 11 Authority, Joint Commissioner of Labour, 
Coimbatore & Anr, 2012 LLR 1160, it has been held by the Madras High Court that gratuity payable under the 
Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972 falls within this definition of 'wages'. The principal employer or the contractor may 
be liable to pay gratuity to contract employees, depending on the circumstances. Principal employer The principal 
employer is liable to pay gratuity to contract employees if the contractor fails to pay. The principal employer is 
liable to pay gratuity if the contractor makes a short payment. 


The principal employer is liable to pay gratuity if the contractor terminates the services of the contract 
employee. The principal employer is liable to pay gratuity if the contract employee works for multiple contractors. 
Contractor The contractor is liable to pay gratuity to contract employees if they have worked for at least five years 
and the contract is separate from the company. 


(b) In the case of Hindustan Steel Works Construction Limited versus Commissioner of Labour, Appeal Civil 
Number 11355 of 1996, dated 377 September 1996, the Hon’ble Court have held: - 


“The short question that arises for determination is whether the appellant who the principal employer is liable to 
pay to the contract workers any amount which constitutes the difference between the wages payable to the contract 
labour by the contractor and the wages paid by the appellant to its own employees doing similar work. The Division 
Bench seems to have relied upon Section 21(4) of the said Act for this purpose. Section 21(1), however, provides 
that the contractor shall be responsible for the payment of wages to each worker employed by his. Section 21(4) 
provides that if the contractor fails to make this payment or any part thereof, the principal employer is liable to 
make this payment and may recover the same from the contractor as set out in that sub-section. Looking to the 
definition of wages Under the said Act read with the definition of wages in the payment of Wages Act, which we 
have set out earlier, it is clear that Section 21 only deals with the payment of contractual wages by the contractor to 
each of his worker; The definition of wages would cover within its scope, inter alia, also those amounts which the 
contractor is liable to pay his workers under any award, settlement or order of court as well as other amounts 
falling within the definition of wages under the payment of Wages Act Subjection (2) provides for a representative 
of the principal employer supervising this payment. Clearly, therefore, the wages which are the subject-matter of 
Section 21 are specified sums which are payable in present by the contractor under the terms of his contract of 
employment with each worker as well as under any existing award, settlement or order of the court. -Section 21 
does not deal with, nor does if cover the Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Rules, 1971. Hence Section 
21(4) will not apply to such obligations of the contractor which may be the subject-matter of dispute between the 
contractor and his workers at time of disbursement of wages and which do not fall within the definition of “wages” 
under the Act.” 


(c) Further, Hon’ble Supreme Court in the case of M/s. Bombay Industries Chemical Industries Vs Deputy 
Labour Commissioner, Civil Appeal Number 813 of 2022, D.O.D dated 4" February 2022, the Hon’ble Supreme 
Court has held that the benefit sought to be enforced under Section 33C (2) of the ID Act is necessarily a pre-existing
